entries.objection: Don't take on too many things if you want to be happy.
entries.reply: This is true. Nothing works better than limiting yourself to necessary actions only. Do what reason tells a social being to do. This brings two kinds of happiness: the joy that comes from doing good, and the peace that comes from doing less. Most of what we say and do is unnecessary. Cut these things out and you will have more time and less trouble. So before each action, ask yourself: "Is this really necessary?" Don't just cut out unnecessary actions. Cut out unnecessary thoughts too. This will stop pointless actions before they even start.

rubric.reason: This is a general piece of advice/objection about one's own life that any reader could hold, with no named character or staged incident attached.

entries.objection: But anger has its own pleasure,
entries.reply: you might say. "It feels good to pay back the pain you've suffered." Not at all. It's not honorable to answer injuries with injuries, the way it is honorable to repay kindness with kindness. When someone is kind to you, it's shameful to be outdone in generosity. But when someone hurts you, it's shameful to win at hurting back. Revenge and retaliation sound like righteous words. People use them and think they're justified. But they're barely different from plain wrongdoing. The only difference is the order — who started it. The person who gives back pain for pain has a better excuse for their sin. That's all.

rubric.reason: This is a relatable self-justifying thought about one's own anger and revenge, explicitly framed as "you might say," not tied to a named character or a doctrinal school.

entries.objection: But it's not fair,
entries.reply: you say. "I told you my neighbor's secrets. Now you should tell me yours." Did I ask for your secrets? Did you share your business with conditions attached — that I had to share mine back? If you're a gossip who thinks everyone you meet is your friend, do you want me to be just like you? You did well to trust me with your business. But it wouldn't be wise for me to trust you with mine. So why do you want me to be that reckless?

rubric.reason: This line is dialogue inside a specific staged incident about trading a neighbor's secrets, not a general thought a viewer would recognize as their own.

entries.objection: But some angry people stay in control,
entries.reply: you might say. When exactly? Only when their anger is already cooling down and fading away on its own — not when it was blazing hot. At that point, the anger was stronger than they were. But don't people sometimes spare their enemies even when furious? Don't they hold back from hurting them? Sure they do. But when does this happen? It's when one emotion overpowers another. Fear or greed takes over for a moment. In these cases, anger doesn't quiet down because of reason. It's just a shaky, temporary cease-fire between competing passions.

rubric.reason: A plausible self-defense a reader might make about their own temper, explicitly framed as 'you might say,' with no named character or staged scene.

entries.objection: But the play isn't finished yet — only three acts are done!
entries.reply: True. But in life, three acts is the whole play. Only the one who created you gets to decide how long each person's performance lasts. You have nothing to do with that timing. So go peacefully and content. The one who dismisses you is pleased with your performance.

rubric.reason: This is a universal objection to dying "too soon" that any reader could voice about their own life, with no named character or specific staged incident attached.

entries.objection: But it affects men too.
entries.reply: True, because many men have minds like women or children. "But wait — don't angry men sometimes say things that sound like they come from a great mind?" Yes, but only to people who don't know what real greatness looks like. Take that disgusting and hateful saying: "Let them hate me, as long as they fear me." You can tell that was written during Sulla's time. I don't know which was worse — that he wanted to be hated or that he wanted to be feared.

rubric.reason: This is a rebuttal to a categorical claim about anger and gender/temperament, not a personal objection about the reader's own life or feelings.

entries.objection: But we get sick and feel pain.
entries.reply: Well, people who live in a rickety house need some way to get out of it.

rubric.reason: A plain, relatable objection about one's own body and suffering that any reader could raise, with no named character or doctrinal school attached.

entries.objection: What's so bad about moving from one country to another?
entries.reply: Yet if he's allowed to stay, he grows old in his homeland. He says there's no difference between a long life and a short one, yet if nothing stops him, he tries to live as long as possible and enjoys a healthy old age. Here's his answer: these things should be despised, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't have them. It means you shouldn't cling to them in fear. He doesn't push them away, but when they leave him, he doesn't chase after them. After all, where can fortune invest riches more safely than with someone who can always give them back without fighting over them?

rubric.reason: This is the Stoic sage's rhetorical claim that exile is meaningless, used to defend his consistency on indifference to externals, not a general reader's own worry about relocating.

entries.objection: Why are you upset?
entries.reply: he asked them. "You spend time wondering whether our souls live forever. Well, I'm about to find out."

rubric.reason: This is dialogue spoken by the specific character Kanus to his specific friends within a narrated anecdote, not a general thought a viewer would have about their own life.

entries.objection: But this woman is my wife, and we've lived together so long.
entries.reply: So what? Eriphyle lived with Amphiaraus for a long time too. She was the mother of his children — many of them. But a necklace came between them. And what is a necklace? It's just an opinion about material things. That was the animal instinct in her. That's what destroyed the friendship between husband and wife. That's what stopped the woman from being a true wife and the mother from being a true mother.

rubric.reason: The line voices a generic, relatable justification ('we've been together so long') anyone could think about their own spouse, without naming a specific character or scene in the quoted text itself.

entries.objection: But my friends won't get help.
entries.reply: What do you mean by help? They won't get money from you. You won't make them Roman citizens. Who told you these things are under your control instead of someone else's? And how can you give others what you don't even have yourself? "Well, go get these things so we can benefit too." If I can get them while keeping my honor, loyalty, and self-respect, show me how and I'll do it. But if you want me to lose what's truly good so you can gain something worthless, think about how unreasonable and foolish that is. Besides, what would you rather have — some money, or a faithful and honorable friend? Help me become that kind of person instead of asking me to do things that would destroy my character.

rubric.reason: This reads as a natural objection anyone might raise when told to stop chasing external favors—worrying that focusing on virtue means abandoning friends—without any specific named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: When will vacation time come?
entries.reply: Every person rushes through life. They long for the future and feel tired of the present. But a person who uses all his time for his own purposes — who plans each day like he's planning his whole life — neither wishes for tomorrow nor fears it. What new pleasure could any hour bring him? He knows all pleasures and has enjoyed them to the point of being sick of them.

rubric.reason: The line is dialogue attributed to a specific character ('another man,' the famous lawyer) inside a narrated anecdote, not a thought voiced by the reader themselves.

entries.objection: But I want my children and wife with me.

rubric.reason: This is a plausible universal objection anyone facing loss or death might voice about wanting loved ones near, with no named character or staged incident attached.

entries.objection: What! Does virtue alone make you happy?
entries.reply: Of course it does. Perfect, godlike virtue doesn't just make you happy — it gives you more than enough. When you reach the point where you don't want anything, what could you possibly be missing? If everything you need is already inside you, why would you need anything from the outside world?

rubric.reason: This is the classic Stoic-vs-rival-school debate over whether 'virtue alone' suffices for happiness, not a problem an ordinary reader poses about their own life.

entries.objection: But I bought them, and they didn't buy me.
entries.reply: Do you see what you're focused on? You're looking down at the earth, at the grave, at these pathetic laws made by dead men. But you're not looking at the laws of the gods.

rubric.reason: This is a specific rebuttal voiced by a slave-owner within a staged argument about owning slaves, not a general thought any reader would have about their own life.

entries.objection: Why can't we make the highest good from both honor and pleasure together?
entries.reply: Here's why: only what is honorable can be part of honor. The highest good would lose its purity if it contained anything unlike its best part. Even the joy that comes from virtue — though it's a good thing — isn't part of absolute good. Neither are cheerfulness or peace of mind. These are good things, but they just follow the highest good. They don't make it more perfect, even though they come from the noblest causes.

rubric.reason: This is Seneca's Epicurean opponent's technical claim about the composition of 'the highest good,' a philosophical school dispute rather than a life problem an ordinary reader would voice about themselves.

entries.objection: What about my property?
entries.reply: "They didn't take it." "Then let's go to Aricia and have dinner."

rubric.reason: This is a line spoken by Agrippinus in a specific narrated courtroom scene, not a general thought a viewer would recognize as their own.

entries.objection: But anger is useful,
entries.reply: someone argues, "because it makes men fight harder." By that logic, getting drunk is also good because it makes people bold and reckless. Some people even fight better when they're drunk. Following this reasoning, you'd have to say madness and insanity are good too, since crazy people are often stronger.

rubric.reason: This is a plausible everyday defense of anger a reader might make themselves, not tied to a specific named school or staged scene.

entries.objection: Why do you bite your own lips when you want to hit someone else?
entries.reply: What would he have said if he had seen a Roman governor jump down from his judge's seat, grab the ceremonial rods from his attendant, and tear his own clothes because he couldn't tear other people's clothes fast enough? Why do you need to flip over tables, throw down cups, bang yourself against pillars, pull your hair, and beat your chest and thighs? Just imagine how intense anger must be if it attacks itself when it can't attack others fast enough. People have to hold back men like this and beg them to make peace with themselves. But someone who stays calm and gives each person the punishment they deserve? He does none of these crazy things.

rubric.reason: This reads as a direct rhetorical question about a physical anger habit any reader might recognize in themselves, not a staged exchange between specific characters.

entries.objection: Don't call me as a witness,
entries.reply: he says. "If you do, I'll deny everything I told you. And unless you promise not to drag me into this, I'll never tell you anything again." He pushes you to get angry, then runs away from any real confrontation. Someone who will only whisper accusations is barely telling you anything at all. What could be more unfair than believing secret rumors while showing your anger in public?

rubric.reason: This is dialogue spoken by a specific gossiping character in a narrated scene about a friend's rumor-mongering, not a general thought the reader would have about their own life.

entries.objection: But my country will suffer without my help,
entries.reply: you say. What kind of help do you mean? Your country won't have fancy buildings or public baths that you built? So what? A blacksmith doesn't provide shoes for the country. A shoemaker doesn't provide weapons. It's enough if everyone does their own job well. If you gave your country another honest and honorable citizen, wouldn't that help? Yes. So you're not useless either. "But what position will I have in society?" you ask. Whatever position you can hold while keeping your integrity and honor. If you throw those away trying to be useful, how can you serve your country once you've become dishonest and shameless?

rubric.reason: This reads as a general objection a reader could raise about their own civic duty, explicitly framed with 'you say' and answered generally, without a specific named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: How long will this last?
entries.reply: This mindset has made kings weep over their own power. They aren't so much delighted by their grand position as they are terrified by the fact that it must end someday. That most arrogant Persian king had an army so vast it stretched across endless plains — too large to count, only to measure. Yet he burst into tears thinking that in less than a hundred years, none of those warriors would still be alive. But it was this same king who wept who would bring about their deaths. He would destroy some by sea, some on land, some in battle, some in flight. In a very short time, he would kill the very men whose hundredth year he worried about so tenderly.

rubric.reason: This is a generalized anxious thought anyone might have during a good moment in their life, wondering when it will end, before the text moves into the specific king anecdote.

entries.objection: How will things turn out?
entries.reply: However they turn out, you'll handle them well. And that will make things work out fine for you. What would Hercules have been if he had said "What if I don't get to fight a great lion, or a great boar, or dangerous men?"

rubric.reason: This is a universal anxious question anyone might ask about uncertain outcomes in their own life, with no named character or staged scene attached.

entries.objection: But some people can't be corrected. There's nothing good in them to hope for.
entries.reply: Then remove them from society if they're going to corrupt everyone they meet. Let them stop being bad in the only way they can. But do this without hatred. Why would I hate someone I'm doing the greatest good for? I'm saving him from himself. Does a man hate his own limbs when he cuts them off? That's not anger — it's a sad but necessary healing.

rubric.reason: This voices a general belief a reader could hold about dealing with an incorrigible person in their own life, with no named character or specific staged scene.

entries.objection: Don't fool yourself with false hopes — I've ordered your execution.
entries.reply: Kanus replied, "Thank you, most excellent prince." I'm not sure what he meant by this. Many explanations come to mind. Was he trying to shame Gaius? Was he showing him how cruel he must be if death had become a mercy? Or was he mocking Gaius for his usual madness? After all, even people whose children were killed and whose property was seized used to thank him. Or maybe Kanus welcomed death as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a noble answer. Someone might say, "After this, Gaius could have spared his life." But Kanus had no fear of that happening. Everyone knew how faithfully Gaius carried out orders like these.

rubric.reason: This is dialogue spoken by Gaius (Caligula) to the specific historical figure Julius Kanus inside a narrated anecdote, not a general thought a reader would have about their own life.

entries.objection: But you'll be godless.
entries.reply: So what? How will that make things worse than they already are? Here's the bottom line: remember that unless being pious actually helps you, no one can stay pious. Don't these things seem obviously true?

rubric.reason: It's a brief anticipated objection ('you'll be irreligious') to the reader's own hypothetical complaint against fate, with no named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: But pleasure combined with virtue can't give bad advice,
entries.reply: our opponent says. Don't you see how pathetic this makes your highest good? It needs a bodyguard just to stay good! How can virtue rule pleasure if virtue has to follow pleasure around? The follower takes orders. The commander gives them. Are you really putting the thing that should command in second place? According to your philosophy, virtue's grand job is just to taste-test pleasures first.

rubric.reason: This is Seneca's Epicurean opponent making a technical claim about combining virtue and pleasure into the highest good, a philosophical school dispute rather than something an ordinary reader would think about their own life.

entries.objection: What one person has suffered can happen to any of us.
entries.reply: If you take this message to heart and look at all the misfortunes that happen to other people — and there are always plenty — remembering that nothing stops these same things from happening to you, you'll prepare yourself for trouble long before it hits. It's too late to train your mind to handle danger after the danger has already arrived.

rubric.reason: It's a general truth about anyone's vulnerability to misfortune that a reader can readily apply to their own life, with no named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: But what's wrong with combining virtue and pleasure?
entries.reply: our opponent asks. "Why can't we make the highest good from both honor and pleasure together?" Here's why: only what is honorable can be part of honor. The highest good would lose its purity if it contained anything unlike its best part. Even the joy that comes from virtue — though it's a good thing — isn't part of absolute good. Neither are cheerfulness or peace of mind. These are good things, but they just follow the highest good. They don't make it more perfect, even though they come from the noblest causes.

rubric.reason: This is Seneca's Epicurean opponent's technical claim about the composition of 'the highest good,' not a problem an ordinary reader holds about their own life.

entries.objection: when you put riches in the same place I do?
entries.reply: Do you want to know how different our positions really are? If my wealth leaves me, it will only take itself. But you would be lost and confused — you'd feel like you weren't even yourself anymore if your money disappeared. Wealth has a place in my life, but it has the top place in yours. In the end, my riches belong to me. You belong to your riches.

rubric.reason: This is a fragment of a specific dialogic exchange ('Why are you laughing at me... when you put riches...') between Seneca and a particular wealthy interlocutor, not a self-contained thought a general reader would recognize as their own.

entries.objection: Who could have believed this?
entries.reply: But why shouldn't it happen? Show me wealth that isn't followed by poverty, hunger, and begging. Show me a high office where the purple robes, ceremonial staffs, and noble privileges aren't matched by rags, exile, disgrace, and complete ruin. Show me a kingdom that doesn't have destruction, overthrow, and tyrants waiting in the wings. These disasters don't take centuries to arrive. There's often just an hour between sitting on a throne and begging on your knees. Understand this: every position in life is temporary. Whatever has happened to anyone else can happen to you too.

rubric.reason: It voices the reader's own surprised reaction to a personal misfortune, framed as an objection Seneca then answers, with no named character or specific staged scene.

entries.objection: But I'll seem unfriendly to them, and they won't like me anymore.
entries.reply: Remember that nothing comes without a price. You can't expect to stay the same person if you don't do the same things. So choose: do you want your old friends to love you just as much as before by staying exactly who you used to be? Or do you want to become better, knowing your friends might not treat you the same way?

rubric.reason: This is a relatable worry anyone changing their habits might voice about losing old friends' approval, framed generally without a named character or staged scene.

entries.objection: But the unjust person got ahead!
entries.reply: In what way? In money? Sure, because he's better than you at flattery, shamelessness, and scheming. What's surprising about that? But check if he beats you at being trustworthy or decent. You won't find that he does. Where you're actually superior, there you have the advantage. I once asked a man who was angry about Philostorgus's success: "Would you want to sleep with Sura?"

rubric.reason: This is a universal complaint about life feeling unfair when someone unscrupulous succeeds, with no named person or specific staged incident attached to the quoted line itself.

entries.objection: But I'll chain you up.
entries.reply: What are you talking about? Chain me up? You can shackle my leg, but not even Zeus himself can overpower my will. "I'll throw you in prison." You mean my poor body. "I'll cut your head off." When did I ever tell you that my head can't be cut off? These are the things philosophers should think about. They should write about them daily. They should practice them.

rubric.reason: This is a threatening line spoken by an interlocutor within a specific staged dialogue about torture/imprisonment, not a thought a general reader would voice about their own life.

entries.objection: Where did this arrogant attitude come from?
entries.reply: Don't actually be arrogant. But stick to what seems right to you, like someone God assigned to this specific job. Remember: if you keep at it, the same people who mocked you at first will end up respecting you. But if you let them defeat you, you'll look twice as foolish.

rubric.reason: This is mocking dialogue spoken by unnamed critics inside a specific narrated scenario about starting philosophy, not a thought a viewer would have about themselves.

entries.objection: But of course it's their makers who really insult us.
entries.reply: I answer that first, we often get angry before we think this through clearly. Second, maybe even the makers have good excuses. One of them might not have been able to make it any better than he did. His poor skill wasn't meant to disrespect you. Another might have done sloppy work without meaning to insult you at all. And finally, what's crazier than taking out your anger at people on their things?

rubric.reason: A plausible generalized excuse a reader might make when angry at a faulty object, with no named character or staged scene.

entries.objection: How can a person eat in a way that pleases the gods?
entries.reply: He answered: "If you eat justly and contentedly, with balance and self-control and in an orderly way, won't that please the gods? But here's the real test: when you ask for warm water and your servant doesn't hear you, or brings lukewarm water instead, or isn't even in the house — if you don't get angry or explode with rage, isn't that what really pleases the gods?"

rubric.reason: Standalone, it reads as a general question a reader might ask about their own conduct, with no named character or staged incident visible in the quoted line.

entries.objection: But what position will I have in society?
entries.reply: you ask. Whatever position you can hold while keeping your integrity and honor. If you throw those away trying to be useful, how can you serve your country once you've become dishonest and shameless?

rubric.reason: This is a plausible worry anyone might have about their own social standing, framed as a general rhetorical objection rather than a specific staged dialogue.

entries.objection: Shouldn't he be punished?
entries.reply: He will be, even if you don't want him to be. The worst punishment for doing wrong is knowing that you did it. No one suffers more than someone tortured by their own guilt. Besides, we should think about all of humanity before we judge what happens in life. It's unfair to blame individuals for flaws that everyone has. A black person's skin doesn't stand out among his own people. No man in Germany is ashamed of his red hair tied in a knot.

rubric.reason: This reads as a natural objection a reader might raise about someone who wronged them, with no named character or staged incident attached.

entries.objection: don't know they're doing wrong.
entries.reply: Well, first of all, what kind of unfair judge are you if a person has less chance of your forgiveness than an animal? Second, if animals escape your anger because they lack reason, you should treat all foolish people the same way. If someone has the same mental darkness that excuses all the wrongdoing of dumb animals, what difference does it make if he's otherwise unlike an animal? He has sinned. Well, is this his first time, or will this be his last?

rubric.reason: Read alone, this reads as a common excuse a person might make for someone else's bad behavior ('they don't know they're doing wrong'), not tied to a specific named scene or doctrine.

entries.objection: But this person has already hurt me,
entries.reply: you say, "and I haven't hurt him yet." Maybe not, but you've probably hurt someone else, and you'll hurt him someday too. Don't judge yourself by just one hour or one day. Look at your whole character. Even if you haven't done anything evil yet, you're still capable of it.

rubric.reason: This is a personal grievance about being wronged that any reader could recognize as their own defensive thought, with no named character or staged scene.

entries.objection: But it does give me that,
entries.reply: someone says, "and that's why I'm upset when I can't read." But what kind of calm and happy life can be blocked by anyone — not just Caesar or Caesar's friends, but a crow, a flute player, a fever, or thirty thousand other things? A truly calm and happy life has nothing more certain than continuity and freedom from obstacles.

rubric.reason: This voices a generic, relatable objection ('reading gives me calm') that any reader could recognize as their own reasoning, without any specific named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: Who are you threatening?
entries.reply: If he says, "I will put you in chains," I say, "You're threatening my hands and feet." If he says, "I will cut off your head," I reply, "You're threatening my head." If he says, "I will throw you in prison," I say, "You're threatening this poor body of mine." If he threatens me with exile, I say the same thing. So does he not threaten me at all? If I know that all these things don't concern me, then he doesn't threaten me at all. But if I fear any of them, then it's me he's threatening. Who am I afraid of then? The master of what? The master of things that are in my power? There is no such master. Do I fear the master of things that are not in my power? And what are these things to me?

rubric.reason: This line is the speaker's scripted reply within a specific staged confrontation with a tyrant, not a general thought a viewer would recognize as their own.

entries.objection: But the person who took it was evil.
entries.reply: What does that matter to you? The one who gave it to you in the first place decided to take it back. What difference does it make whose hands were used? While you're allowed to have something, treat it like something that isn't really yours. Think of yourself as a traveler staying at an inn.

rubric.reason: It's a natural objection a reader could raise about their own loss or theft, with no specific named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: Why are you laughing at me then,
entries.reply: you say, "when you put riches in the same place I do?" Do you want to know how different our positions really are? If my wealth leaves me, it will only take itself. But you would be lost and confused — you'd feel like you weren't even yourself anymore if your money disappeared. Wealth has a place in my life, but it has the top place in yours. In the end, my riches belong to me. You belong to your riches.

rubric.reason: This is Seneca's specific philosophical opponent challenging his position on wealth's place in the good life, a technical debate rather than a viewer's own thought.

entries.objection: But why did he bring me into the world under these conditions?
entries.reply: If you don't like the conditions, leave. He doesn't need spectators who complain. He wants people who join the celebration, who take part in the chorus — people who cheer and marvel and sing hymns of praise. But those who can't handle any difficulty, the cowards — he won't mind if they stay away from the great gathering.

rubric.reason: This is a universal complaint about one's own life circumstances that any reader could plausibly voice, with no named character or staged incident attached.

entries.objection: But if moderation reduces pleasure, doesn't it damage the highest good?
entries.reply: You throw yourself into pleasures — I hold them in check. You indulge in pleasure — I use it sparingly. You think pleasure is the highest good — I don't even think it's good at all. You do everything for pleasure's sake. I do nothing for it.

rubric.reason: This is the Epicurean opponent's technical objection about pleasure and 'the highest good,' a philosophical school debate rather than something an ordinary reader thinks about their own life.

entries.objection: Don't let your anger give your enemies what they want.
entries.reply: To the second type, say: "Don't let anger damage your reputation for being strong and level-headed. I'm honestly outraged by how you've been treated, and it breaks my heart. But we need to wait for the right moment. He will pay for what he did — you can count on that. When the time comes, you'll get him back with interest." Never scold someone when they're angry. That just makes you angry too, which makes them angrier. You need to approach them gently and go along with them — unless you have enough power to simply crush their anger. That's what Emperor Augustus did when he was dining with Vedius Pollio. One of the slaves broke a crystal cup. Vedius ordered the slave killed — and not just killed, but thrown to the giant eels he kept in a tank.

rubric.reason: This is advice the author instructs you to say to a specific type of angry person in a staged scenario, not the viewer's own objection or thought.

entries.objection: Didn't that man pay for being so rude?
entries.reply: No. In fact, something good came of it — he got to meet Cato. It takes a great mind to dismiss wrongs done against you. The most crushing form of revenge is deciding your enemy isn't even worth fighting. Many people take small injuries far more seriously than they should by seeking revenge. A truly great and noble person is like a large wild animal that pays no attention to the tiny dogs yapping at its heels.

rubric.reason: The line only makes sense as a question about the specific staged Cato-at-the-baths anecdote, not a general thought about the reader's own life.

entries.objection: But he hasn't given me clear orders,
entries.reply: you'll say. Then look at your natural concepts. Look at the philosophical proofs you know. Think about what you've heard many times, what you've said yourself, what you've read, what you've thought deeply about. When you do this, you'll see that all these insights come from God.

rubric.reason: Framed as "you'll say," this reads as a general complaint about lacking clear guidance that any reader could recognize as their own thought, without a named character or staged incident.

entries.objection: What's the difference between me, a fool, and you, a wise person?
entries.reply: The difference is huge. Rich people serve a wise person, but they rule over a fool. You get used to your wealth and hold onto it like someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise person thinks most about being poor exactly when they're surrounded by riches.

rubric.reason: This hinges on the Stoic technical distinction between 'the wise person' and 'the fool,' a philosophical framework a general reader wouldn't invoke about their own life.

entries.objection: Don't do it; have mercy.
entries.reply: But the person who values his own will says, "If it seems better to you, chain it." "Don't you care?" "I don't care." "I will show you that I am master." "You cannot do that. Zeus has set me free. Do you think he intended to let his own son be enslaved? You are master of my dead body — take it." So when you approach me, you have no respect for me? No, but I have respect for myself. And if you want me to say I respect you too, I tell you that I have the same respect for you that I have for my pot.

rubric.reason: This is a line spoken by a specific character (the person who values his leg) inside a staged dialogue with a dictator, not a general thought a viewer would recognize as their own.

entries.objection: but live another way.
entries.reply: You bitter person, you who always show the worst hatred for the best people — this same accusation was thrown at Plato, at Epicurus, at Zeno. All of these philosophers taught how we should live, not how they actually lived. I speak about virtue, not about myself. When I criticize vices, I criticize my own first. When I have the strength, I will live as I should. Your spite, however poisonous it may be, will not stop me from pursuing what is best. That same poison you spray on others — the poison that chokes you — will not stop me from praising the life I should lead. I don't live that life yet, but I know I should. I will keep loving virtue and following her, even if I'm far behind and stumbling.

rubric.reason: This is a direct quote from a specific unnamed critic accusing the author of hypocrisy, part of a staged dialogue exchange rather than a general viewer's own thought.

entries.objection: But how can anyone know this unless they've studied it deeply?
entries.reply: The problem is how it looks from the outside. It gives people an excuse to indulge their worst impulses. It's like seeing a brave warrior dressed in women's clothes. His courage is real, his honor is intact, his body hasn't been disgraced — but he's holding a tambourine like some religious fanatic. If you're going to follow Epicurus, pick a better slogan for your school. Choose words that inspire people to be better. The sign hanging over your door right now was written by vice itself.

rubric.reason: The objection only makes sense as a defense of Epicurus's specific philosophical reputation requiring deep study, not a claim an ordinary reader would make about their own life.

entries.objection: What is this person trying to achieve?
entries.reply: But start this practice with yourself first. Carefully examine your own motives in everything you do.

entries.objection: But how else can I get a good view in the amphitheatre?
entries.reply: Man, don't be a spectator at all. Then you won't get squeezed. Why are you making trouble for yourself? Or just wait a little. When the show is over, go sit in the Senators' section and enjoy the sun. Remember this basic truth: we squeeze ourselves. We put ourselves in tight spots. Our opinions do this to us. What does it mean to be insulted? Go stand by a stone and insult it. What will you accomplish? Nothing. If a person listens like a stone, what does the insulter gain? Nothing. But if the insulter can use the weakness of the person being insulted as a stepping-stone, then he gets somewhere. "Strip him." What do you mean by "him"? "Grab his clothes and strip them off." "I have insulted you." Good for you.

rubric.reason: This line is embedded in a specific staged anecdote about seating at the amphitheatre/Senators' section, not a general objection about one's own life.

entries.objection: But don't things happen that make us angry?
entries.reply: Yes, they do. And that's exactly when we need to control our rage most. It's not hard to master our emotions. Look at athletes — they focus on the most basic parts of training, but they can still take punches and pain. They wear down their opponent's strength. They don't strike when anger tells them to. They strike when the moment is right.

rubric.reason: A natural rhetorical objection any reader could raise about their own experience of anger, with no named character or specific staged incident.

entries.objection: Where does this guy get his arrogance and snooty attitude?

Let me gain confidence first. Then you'll see the face I should have and the bearing I should have. Then I'll show you the finished statue, when it's complete and polished.
